title: Hayden Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Hayden wells have a 30-foot median depth, but fractured bedrock makes yield and drilling cost vary widely.
h1: What Hayden, Colorado Wells Are Really Like
intro_html:
Buying land near Hayden means paying close attention to the well record, not just the listing description. Within 5 miles of Hayden, Colorado, DWR records include 445 permitted wells. Of those, 249 are recorded as constructed, 243 report total depth, 33 report pump yield, and 41 report static water level.

The local pattern is unusual for a mountain area: the median recorded well is only 30 feet deep, while the middle half runs from 15 to 240 feet. Most permits identify an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer. That combination means one nearby shallow well may not predict the result on the next lot.

sections.heading: Hayden’s well depths range from shallow to very deep
sections.html:
Recorded depth near Hayden has a 30-foot median, with the middle half between 15 and 240 feet. The depth spread matters more than the median when you are asking for a drilling bid. A driller may encounter shallow water in one location and fractured rock requiring a much deeper hole a short distance away.

The depth mix shows that 64% of recorded wells are under 100 feet. Another 14% are 100 to 300 feet deep, 17% fall between 300 and 600 feet, and 5% exceed 600 feet. The 90th-percentile depth is 429 feet, and the deepest record is 3,086 feet.

Most permits name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer. Granite and gneiss can produce water through fractures rather than through a uniform underground layer, so neighboring well depths are useful evidence but not a guarantee.

sections.heading: What Hayden wells produce for a household
sections.html:
Only 33 wells in the records report a pump yield, so the yield statistics are a limited local sample. Among those reports, the median is 8.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 5.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute.

Six percent of reported yields are under 1 gallon per minute. Another 12% are between 1 and 5 gallons per minute, while 48% fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute and 33% exceed 15 gallons per minute. A result under 1 gallon per minute is a serious constraint for a residence unless storage and the intended use are designed around it.

Ask for the well-construction report, pump test information, storage capacity, and permitted use. A strong-looking yield does not by itself confirm that a proposed household use is legally covered.

sections.heading: The water level looks shallow, but the trend is limited
sections.html:
Only 41 wells report a static water level. In that group, the median depth to water is 5 feet, and the middle half is 4 to 6 feet. Those figures suggest shallow reported water levels in the sampled wells, but they do not describe every parcel or guarantee that water will be reached at the same elevation.

The permit counts by decade do not show a water-level trend; they show when permits were issued. Records include 4 permits from the 1950s, 1 from the 1960s, 34 from the 1970s, 36 from the 1980s, 77 from the 1990s, 52 from the 2000s, 46 from the 2010s, and 73 from the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025.

For a purchase, compare static water levels from nearby wells and ask whether measurements were taken before or after pumping.

sections.heading: Who has drilled around Hayden, and when
sections.html:
Hayden’s permit history is spread across several decades, with the largest recorded decade being the 1990s at 77 permits. The 2020s account for 73 permits, and the newest permit year in the records is 2025. That recent activity means nearby records may be more useful than relying only on older ranch or household wells.

The most active driller names in the records are Authorized (Pe, Pg), associated with 70 wells; Routt Drilling Co. (Ozbun, Jerald A.), associated with 36; and Aztec Drilling Company (Branstetter, Keith), associated with 14. These names describe permit records, not a guarantee of current availability or workmanship.

Before closing, pull the actual DWR permits for neighboring parcels. Check construction dates, casing and grout details, reported depth, pump yield, and permitted use. A permit is not the same as a successful production test.

sections.heading: What a new Hayden well may cost
sections.html:
Local drilling conditions are modeled as fractured mountain bedrock, including granite and gneiss. The stated drilling rate is $65 to $100 per foot. At Hayden’s 30-foot median depth, the drilled hole alone models to about $2,000 to $3,000.

A finished system, including the pump, tank, trenching, and electrical work, is modeled at about $8,000 to $15,000. That is a planning range, not a fixed quote. Depth, access, casing and grout requirements, water storage, power distance, and difficult rock can move the final number.

Because 64% of recorded wells are under 100 feet but the deepest record reaches 3,086 feet, ask for a written bid with assumptions and a clear treatment of additional footage. Confirm what happens if the hole is low-yield or dry.

sections.heading: Risks to check before building near Hayden
sections.html:
Low yield is the first practical concern. Six percent of reported pump yields are under 1 gallon per minute, and the available yield sample is small. A dry hole or poor-producing fracture can still occur even where a nearby well performs well.

Environmental records also deserve review. Within about 10 miles, the mapped information includes 14 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 36 historic mine features. There are 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites in the stated data. These records do not prove contamination on a particular parcel, so test the actual well water and check the site history.

Have a septic designer review setbacks from the well, replacement-area needs, slope, soil, and groundwater conditions before placing a house. Confirm access for a drill rig and future service equipment. DWR permits, exempt household-use rules, and any augmentation-plan requirements can affect what the well may legally supply.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Hayden, Colorado?
faq.a: The median recorded well depth within 5 miles of Hayden is 30 feet. The middle half runs from 15 to 240 feet. However, 17% of recorded wells are 300 to 600 feet deep, 5% exceed 600 feet, and the deepest record is 3,086 feet. Fractured mountain bedrock makes the result highly dependent on the specific parcel.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Hayden, Colorado?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $65 to $100 per foot. At the 30-foot median depth, the drilled hole is modeled at about $2,000 to $3,000. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical work is about $8,000 to $15,000. Request a written bid that explains additional footage and dry-hole terms.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce near Hayden?
faq.a: Among the 33 wells reporting pump yield, the median is 8.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 5.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Six percent report under 1 gallon per minute. Because the reporting sample is limited and fractured rock varies, review the actual well test and storage setup before buying.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Hayden, Colorado?
faq.a: The local records identify 14 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 36 historic mine features within about 10 miles, with 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those mapped facts do not establish the quality of one well. Test the property’s water, especially for contaminants suggested by its location and land-use history.

faq.q: Can I build a house on a well near Hayden?
faq.a: A buildable lot needs more than a nearby well record. Check the DWR permit and allowed use, the well’s yield and storage, septic suitability, setbacks, access, and power. Most recorded wells are domestic or household use at 60%, while stock use is 21%. An exempt household-use well has legal limits, so confirm the intended use before designing.
